transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29 16:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Michael Green (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM), Rajesh (CTO, Northbridge), Sofia (Head of ML), Ethan (Security), Maya (Platform), Tom (Product)

Summary (auto):
Client is exploring exit from Azure OpenAI + mixed on-prem v L L M stack. Primary drivers: cost, latency for low-latency trading assistant, and strict data residency / audit requirements. Interested in hosted pilot but needs enterprise security posture for finance (KMS, HSM, audit logs). Wants eval parity with current models and clear runbook for cutover.

Topics: migration path, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, vLLM/T G I compatibility, security controls (KMS/HSM, SSO), benchmarking and pilot scope.

[00:00] Michael (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros — I'm Michael, AE at Redwood, with Priya our solutions engineer and Liam on success. over to you Rajesh for a sec to frame why you're evaluating options now

[00:18] Rajesh (CTO): Yeah thanks uh Michael. So basically we're running a mixed stack today, majority on Azure OpenAI for chat and some in-house inference with v L L M for lower latency. We're seeing costs spike and some inconsistency in latency because we have bursts during market open. Also compliance is tightening so we need better auditability and control.

[00:44] Sofia (Head of ML): And from an ML perspective we care about parity — we have a set of eval prompts that must produce equivalent quality to our current Anthropic and OpenAI baselines. If switching infra changes hallucination or scoring, that's a blocker.

[01:05] Priya (Redwood SE): Totally, that's exactly what Redwood's migration playbook focuses on — we look at inference parity, perf, and operational controls. Quick question: are you running quantized weights on v L L M today or full precision?

[01:18] Maya (Platform): We're doing int8 quant on the v L L M hosts, and those are colocated in our colo as part of a private cluster. The Azure endpoints are public but restricted with IP allowlists.

[01:35] Ethan (Security): For us the critical items are: KMS integration (customer-managed keys), detailed audit logs for every request, SSO/SAML access control, and ability to run in a private VPC or on-prem without egress to public internet. Also we need SOC2 plus evidence of encryption at rest and in transit.

[01:55] Michael: Good — those are standard asks, we support customer K M S and H S M integrations, RBAC via S S O SAML and fine-grained audit logs in the Redwood Console. For private deployments there's a private control-plane option with no egress by default. Priya, do you want to cover the hosting options briefly?

[02:12] Priya: Sure. High level: Hosted API — fastest to start, pay-as-you-go; Dedicated — reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and SLA, still managed by Redwood but isolated to your tenancy; Private — we ship a private control plane and optionally on-prem inference nodes for air-gapped needs. In your case the private deployment or dedicated with VPC peering would fit the compliance asks.

[02:38] Tom (Product): Can you run the same model families we use today? Our stack uses GPT-like models and a few Mistral variants. We also have some Llama-based models in-house on v L L M.

[02:51] Priya: Yes, we onboard open model families and can host your exact model artifacts. Note: when moving from Azure OpenAI endpoints there are differences in tokenization and sometimes subtle output shifts — we run eval parity tests using your prompt set and produce delta reports. For Llama variants we also validate K V cache behavior and continuous batching performance.

[03:17] Sofia: The parity tests are key. How do you measure 'equivalent'? We have business thresholds — ROUGE/accuracy and some manual evals.

[03:30] Priya: We do automated evals (BLEU/ROUGE or your chosen metrics), latent embedding similarity checks, and sample human review for edge cases. We also track tail latency and token cost per 1M tokens. We'll produce an eval dashboard so you can compare side-by-side.

[03:50] Rajesh: About perf — our trading assistant needs sub-200ms median for short prompts at peak. Right now v L L M in our colo hits that with int8 quant + optimized kernels. Can Redwood hit that with Dedicated or Private?

[04:08] Priya: For sub-200ms we usually recommend private or dedicated with colocated capacity. Our runtime picks optimized kernels based on sequence length and model architecture; for very low latency we can pin capacity and use smaller seq-length-optimized kernels. There's a tradeoff with batching (more batching reduces cost but increases latency). For 200ms median, continuous KV caching and prefix caching are critical.

[04:38] Ethan: How is K V cache handled? We cannot share KV across tenants but within our cluster we want deterministic caching. Does Redwood support sticky caches and cache invalidation controls?

[04:52] Priya: Yes — cache scoping can be per-customer or per-deployment. We have invalidation APIs and TTL controls. In private mode you control the cache nodes. There might be some transcription in our docs that says 'K V' as spaced letters, apologies, but operationally it's standard KV.

[05:10] Sofia: What about runtime compatibility — we're running T G I adapters in our pipeline and some custom tensors. Does Redwood accept custom op kernels or is it limited?

[05:23] Priya: We support a range of model formats and often accept T G I exports and v L L M checkpoints; for custom ops we collaborate on kernel selection and can add a compatibility shim. There's usually an SE integration effort for custom runtimes.

[05:40] Tom: For the migration, what's a typical pilot? We want to minimize customer-facing risk.

[05:48] Michael: Typical pilot: 4-8 week scoped POC. Weeks 1-2: onboarding, infra setup (dedicated or private), and sample model upload. Weeks 3-4: parity tests with your prompt set, perf benchmarking under synthetic load mirroring peak, and run a small traffic shadowing test. Final 1-2 weeks for analysis, config tuning, and rollback runbook.

[06:15] Rajesh: Shadowing is important. We can't risk user-visible regressions. Does Redwood do canary and automatic fallback to Azure OpenAI?

[06:27] Priya: Yes, routing policies support canary and A/B rollouts and automatic fallback to upstream endpoints when capacity constraints or quality regressions are detected. That's part of the rollout policies in Redwood Console.

[06:40] Ethan: On the security docs — we need to see pen test reports, SOC2 type II, and details on key lifecycle. Also how logs are retained and whether we can ship logs to our SIEM (they use Splunk).

[06:56] Michael: We'll send the security pack; we can also set up an engineering call with our security specialist. Logs can be streamed to your Splunk via our logging connector and we support configurable retention windows and exportable audit trails.

[07:12] Maya: Network-wise, we need VPC peering and maybe transit gateway; NAT egress must be controllable. For private on-prem, do you require outbound calls to Redwood control plane?

[07:26] Priya: Private control plane has a no-egress option. There's an initial management channel for updates which can be configured through your jump box; alternatively we offer a full air-gap option for on-prem packages. We'll need your network diagram to validate firewall ports.

[07:42] Tom: Pricing — rough sketch we need to present to finance. How different is hosted vs dedicated in unit economics?

[07:52] Michael: Hosted is simpler but unit cost is higher; dedicated is reserved capacity with lower per-token price and more predictable latency. Private has a platform/license fee plus infra. We'll supply a sketch based on your current token volumes — Rajesh if you can share monthly token counts that helps.

[08:10] Rajesh: We can share monthly token usage; expect high bursts at market open and end of day. We'll put that in the doc.

[08:18] Priya: Also worth noting quantization differences — when you move from int8 on v L L M to our runtime, we might recommend a quant profile; sometimes small accuracy regressions are observed and we can compensate with model distillation or temperature tweaks. We'll log those deltas in the eval report.

[08:38] Sofia: Potential blocker: we use a custom prompt rewriter and a pre-filter that mutates tokens pre-inference. Does Redwood integrate with our pre/post pipeline?

[08:51] Priya: Yes, you can run pre/post processing in your own service or as step-functions in our routing pipeline; we can host function calls or instrument hooks in the inference path. We'll need examples.

[09:03] Rajesh: On competitors — we've looked at native Azure OpenAI for convenience and Anthropic for safety profiles. Why Redwood vs them?

[09:14] Michael: Two things: first, unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private so you can start hosted and graduate to private without rewriting your stack; second, production controls — strong per-route observability, rollout policies, and cost levers like auto-batching and prefix caching which reduce unit cost. We also do model onboarding for your exact artifacts instead of forcing proprietary formats.

[09:36] Ethan: Auditability again — in the private deployment what does the operator model look like? Who has admin access?

[09:45] Liam (CSM): Admin roles can map to your SAML groups, we support least-privilege roles and an admin audit trail. For enterprise installs we can set up an installation-runbook that outlines operator responsibilities and escalation.

[09:59] Tom: What's the typical time to move from pilot to production?

[10:05] Priya: If the pilot goes well, 2-3 months including rollout, can be faster if you pick hosted+D edicated hybrid. Private on-prem longer due to procurement but we've done sub-8-week private installs for experienced infra teams.

[10:22] Sofia: A couple of gotchas to watch: tokenization differences that change prompt lengths and cost; embedding differences if you rely on semantic search.

[10:32] Priya: We'll run an embedding parity check against your search corpus and include delta metrics. For tokenization, we output tokenized counts so you can reconcile cost.

[10:44] Rajesh: Great. To wrap, let's confirm next steps and owners.

[10:50] Michael: Action items recap: we'll send security docs (Michael), SE will request prompt set and produce baseline perf checklist (Priya), Maya will provide network diagram (Maya), Rajesh will share token volumes (Rajesh). We'll aim for the SE deep-dive next week to scope private network ports and benchmarking.

[11:08] Rajesh: Sounds good. One last question: if we need to fallback to Azure during rollout, is there any risk of data leakage between routes?

[11:18] Priya: No — routing preserves data isolation and we can configure scrubbing when routing to third-party providers. We'll share the routing and data flow doc.

[11:28] Michael: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the SE deep-dive.

[11:34] Sofia: Thanks all.
